                    ### Question
                    A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of abdominal pain and foul-smelling, watery diarrhea for several days. He has not had nausea, vomiting, or blood in the stool. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and recently completed a 7-day course of clindamycin for pneumonia. He has not traveled out of the United States. Which of the following toxins is most likely to be involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Shiga toxin
opb. Cholera toxin
opc. Cereulide toxin
opd. Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin
ope. Alpha toxin

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with abdominal pain and foul-smelling, watery diarrhea after a recent course of clindamycin, which is known to disrupt normal gut flora and increase the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. C. difficile is an opportunistic pathogen that can cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea, characterized by foul-smelling stools due to the production of cytotoxins. The reasoning chains consistently point to C. difficile cytotoxin as the most likely toxin involved in this patient's symptoms, supported by the recent antibiotic use and the nature of the diarrhea. Other toxins listed (Shiga, Cholera, Cereulide, Alpha) are less relevant given the clinical context and presentation. Therefore, the most likely toxin involved is Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin.
